question.text: Which of the following is TRUE about the 'irrevocable' nature of an AIF trust?

answer.text: The sponsor can withdraw the trust property at any time
The ownership of trust property is permanently vested with the trust and cannot be reverted to the settlor
The trust can be dissolved without investor consent
The irrevocable nature can be changed by the manager

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook (p.102) draws the revocable-versus-irrevocable distinction directly: in a revocable trust the trust property can revert to the settlor, whereas in an irrevocable trust ownership of the trust property is permanently vested with the trust and cannot be taken back by the settlor. In the AIF context the sponsor may act as the settlor (p.189), so once the trust is irrevocably settled, the sponsor in that settlor capacity cannot reclaim the corpus. The Trap: Irrevocability does not mean the trust lasts forever or that it can be wound up without following its terms; it speaks only to the inability of the settlor to take back the property. It is not a feature the manager can unilaterally change. Note: Source references: NISM Series XIX-A workbook p.102 (revocable vs irrevocable trust — property reverting vs permanently vested) and p.189 (sponsor may act as settlor).
